---
title: "Curation rationale"
---

ImmPrint exists to score immune processes in transcriptomic data cleanly, and in
a way you can defend. This page sets out the curatorial decisions that shape the
collection.

## Why not just use Hallmark, Reactome or GO?

General-purpose collections are invaluable, but they are built for breadth, not for clean
immune *signatures*. Used directly for module scoring, they tend to
share a few recurring problems:

- **Non-specific drivers.** Stress and activation-response genes (MAPK, ATF, JUN,
  FOS, HSP) recur across many sets, dampening the specificity of module scores.
- **Ligand contamination.** Signalling sets frequently include the very ligand
  that triggers the pathway, either for completeness or to account for autocrine
  signalling in bulk RNA-seq data. However, single-cell RNA-seq allows
  ligand-producing and responding cells to be distinguished. In this context, a
  gene set that carries its own ligand pollutes the score of the cell you actually
  care about.
- **No internal structure.** A single set may fold a receptor, its entire transducer
  cascade, generic stress machinery and dozens of loosely associated targets into
  one undifferentiated list.
- **Unsourced membership.** Membership is rarely traceable to a specific paper
  linking *that* gene to *that* pathway.

## Principle 1 - Mechanistic specificity

Each set aims to capture a single, mechanistically coherent process. Ubiquitous
machinery that carries no pathway-specific information (ribosomal proteins,
proteasome subunits, ubiquitination machinery, core housekeeping genes) is
excluded from every set. The test for each candidate gene is not "is it expressed
when this pathway is active?" but "does its expression *specifically* mark this
process?"

## Principle 2 - Focus on the signal-receiving cell

A set describes the cell *receiving* a signal or *enacting* a process, not the cell
sending it. A pathway's own ligand is **excluded from its own signalling set**,
because the ligand reports on the *sending* cell. The same molecule is **kept**
wherever it is an *output* of the process being measured.

So interferon-gamma is treated differently by context: `IFNG` is **not** a member of
`IMMPRINT_IFNG_SIGNALLING`, but it **is** a legitimate effector of
`IMMPRINT_TYPE1_RESPONSE`. The same logic removes `IL2` from
`IMMPRINT_IL2_SIGNALLING` and `TNF` from `IMMPRINT_TNF_SIGNALLING`, while leaving
inputs, transducers and effectors in place.

The checkpoint sets make this concrete. The inhibitory-receptor sets contain the
receptor and its intrinsic signalling apparatus, and not the ligands presented by the
opposing cell, so PD-L1 and PD-L2 are absent from `IMMPRINT_PD1_SIGNALLING`. These
sets also contain only genes that are *induced or active* in the programme and
exclude genes the pathway *represses*.

## Principle 3 - Cell type specificity

The same ligand drives different programmes in different cells. TGF-β, for
instance, does very different things in T cells, fibroblasts and epithelium.
ImmPrint layers cell type-specific effector refinements onto each pathway's shared
`pan` core, so a cell is scored against the version that matches what it is. These
refinements are added only where the divergence is real and well-documented.

## Principle 4 - Citations you can follow

Every gene set membership carries at least one PubMed ID. The citation should be
primary literature that links that gene to that named pathway. A generic review is
not enough. Where a gene appears in more than one set, each appearance is meant to be
supported by a paper appropriate to that context.

::: callout-note
This is an alpha release. Citations are checked against PubMed where possible, but
some may still need correcting. If you find a citation that does not support its
membership, please [flag it on GitHub](https://github.com/akmclz/immprint/issues)
so it can be fixed in the next version.
:::

## Principle 5 - Corroboration by MSigDB

Where a gene's membership is corroborated by an assigned MSigDB reference gene set
(from Hallmark, Reactome or GO:BP), that set is recorded in `reference_gene_set`. A
blank entry means either the gene is not covered by any MSigDB counterparts or that
there is no valid counterpart.

## Principle 6 - Explicit family exclusions

A few gene families are excluded from **all** sets by standing policy, because they
are general stress or activation responders and not pathway-specific markers:
the `MAPK` families (`MAPK*`, `MAP2K*`, `MAP3K*`) and the `ATF`, `JUN`,
`FOS` and `HSP` families. Excluding them keeps sets from collapsing toward a
generic activation signal.

## The signalling hierarchy annotation

Separately from the principles above, every gene is annotated with a position in a
three-tier hierarchy (`pathway_level`):

- <span style="color:var(--tier-input);font-weight:600">Input (1)</span>: the most
  upstream node *present in the set*. A surface or intracellular receptor where the
  set has one; the driving transcription factor where it does not, as in the MHC,
  proliferation and metabolic sets.
- <span style="color:var(--tier-transducer);font-weight:600">Transducer (2)</span>:
  constitutive signalling machinery — kinases, adaptors, STATs, SMADs, the master
  lineage TF of the set it defines, core processing enzymes and structural complexes.
  The tier carries a claim: *this transcript is largely constitutive and does not
  track pathway activity*. Initiator and inflammatory caspases sit here.
- <span style="color:var(--tier-effector);font-weight:600">Effector (3)</span>: the
  transcriptional output — secreted cytokines and chemokines, cytotoxic and
  antiviral/antimicrobial molecules, presented MHC, induced target-gene products and
  induced regulators. A negative regulator sits here when the pathway it restrains
  transcriptionally induces it (`SOCS3`, `TNFAIP3`, `AXIN2`). It sits at the
  transducer tier when it is constitutive (`AXIN1`, `SKI`, `TREX1`). Direction is recorded
  separately by `regulatory_role`. Executioner caspases sit here.

A gene may hold different tiers in different sets, by design: a master regulator is a
transducer in the set it defines and an effector in the set that induces it, so
`CIITA`, `GATA3`, `TBX21` and `FOXP3` each appear at two tiers across the collection.

## The readout type annotation

Tiers are interpretive metadata and not a universal scoring axis, because not
every pathway is transcriptionally legible. What a score over a set means is recorded
per set in `readout_type`:

- `inducible` — the pathway ends in a transcriptional programme, so the effector tier
  reads out activity. *Does the pathway end in a transcriptional programme whose genes
  are in this set?*
- `state` — the set describes a differentiation state, so score all tiers and read the
  effector tier as phenotype. *Does a high score describe what the
  cell is, or what it is doing right now?*
- `machinery` — the score reflects standing apparatus and makes no activity claim.
  *Is the pathway executed post-translationally, or are its tiers architectural?*

By design, the antigen-receptor and inhibitory-checkpoint sets (TCR, BCR, CTLA4, PD1)
and oxidative phosphorylation carry no effector tier: they are detection, inhibition
or capacity modules that terminate at the transducer level. All are `machinery`.
`IMMPRINT_NLRP3_INFLAMMASOME` is `inducible`, but reports inflammasome *priming*
only — activation itself is post-translational.

## The regulatory role annotation

The tier locates a gene in the cascade; it does not say whether the gene drives the
pathway or holds it back. That direction is recorded separately, per membership, in
`regulatory_role`:

- `none`: a forward component or an output of the pathway. This is most genes,
  including inputs, transducers and effector products.
- `inhibitory`: a negative regulator of the pathway, such as the SOCS and CISH
  negative-feedback proteins, the inhibitory SMADs, the Wnt destruction complex,
  decoy receptors and the anti-apoptotic BCL2 guards.
- `activating`: a positive-feedback amplifier.
- `context_dependent`: the sign genuinely varies, as for `PTPN11` in cytokine
  signalling.

The sign is judged relative to the gene's *own* pathway, which is why it lives on
the membership and not the gene. `IL1RN` is an output of IL-10 even
though it antagonises IL-1, so in `IMMPRINT_IL10_SIGNALLING` it is `none`, not a
negative regulator. `BCL2` opposes intrinsic apoptosis but is a survival output of
IL-7 and IL-15, so it is `inhibitory` in one set and `none` in the others. `PTPN11`
enacts the inhibitory signal in PD1 and CTLA4 but modulates JAK/STAT either way elsewhere.

## Versioning

Each collection is an immutable, versioned snapshot. The gene sets behind a
published analysis can be traced back to the exact definitions used, the way an
MSigDB release is pinned. New curation ships as a new version; released versions
are never altered. See the [changelog](changelog.qmd).

## Intended use

ImmPrint is built for **module scoring** of immune processes, reading out the
activity of specific, mechanistically defined programmes across cell types,
tissues and disease states. The sets are plain, unweighted gene lists, so they
work with any rank-based scoring method (UCell, AUCell, singscore, ssGSEA) and with
average-based methods like `Seurat::AddModuleScore`. See [Access](access.qmd) to get started.
